message.reasoning:
I need to decide on an auction bid for SHORT_LINE.

Opponent p2 currently leads at $90. I have $546 cash and am at WATER_WORKS. The plan is to bid $91 and raise by $1 each turn until $99, then drop out. I am second-guessing whether this strategy is sound.

Railroad mortgage value is $100. Winning the auction for $91–$99 and mortgaging immediately would net $1–$9 profit. I need to confirm whether mortgaging is allowed right after purchase.

I am checking whether mortgaged cash is available before rent is due. I currently own WATER_WORKS, so no rent is owed now. p2 has only $225 and owns dangerous properties: Park Place and Boardwalk with 3 houses each, plus the orange monopoly with 4 houses each. I need to calculate rent amounts to ensure my $546 can survive landing on those spaces.

Boardwalk with three houses costs $1400. Park Place with three houses costs $1100. The orange monopoly’s four-house rent is still being verified.

The orange monopoly’s four-house rent is $750, $750, and $800. My $546 cash cannot cover any of those. I would go bankrupt if I land on orange or dark blue with three houses. I am now calculating the light blue monopoly’s house rent.

Light blue house rent is $450 on Oriental, $270 on Vermont, and $300 on Connecticut. p2 cannot afford any of these with only $225. I am now checking whether p2 can sell houses from their orange monopoly to raise cash.

p2 owns 18 houses total. Selling them would raise cash, since orange and dark blue houses sell for half their purchase price.

If p2 wins the auction and mortgages Short Line, they also gain $1–$9 cash. The bidding strategy therefore does not drain their funds.

The key insight is that dropping out now would gift p2 roughly $10 in arbitrage profit. Bidding to $99 forces them to pay closer to the $100 mortgage value, cutting their free cash extraction by one dollar per bid. Winning at $99 nets only a $1 profit, but it prevents them from gaining the full $10.

I already own two mortgaged railroads. Unmortgaging them plus Short Line would cost 10% interest, so that path is rejected.

Winning at $99 leaves me with $447 cash after the bid, then $547 after mortgaging. That net gain of one dollar is acceptable.

I am now weighing whether p2 might keep bidding past $100 for strategic reasons. They own a mortgaged B&O railroad and may value the Short Line for rent or blocking.

Railroad rent is only $25 for one active railroad, so Short Line offers little strategic value. Both players should value it near the $100 mortgage price.

I am weighing whether to jump straight to $99 to end the auction quickly. If p2 drops out at that price, I win for $99 and gain one dollar after mortgaging. If they continue to $100, I should drop and receive no arbitrage profit.

Bidding $91 would let p2 drop out at a lower price and extract more arbitrage. Jumping straight to $99 risks leaving money on the table if they had folded earlier. Since p2 has matched every bid from $2 to $90, they are committed to extracting the full arbitrage up to mortgage value. The optimal play is to match their strategy and bid $99 or continue one dollar at a time.

I will stick with the incremental +1 bid starting at $91. This is consistent with my established strategy and gives me more profit if p2 drops out early. I am now questioning whether Short Line's mortgage value is actually $100.

Railroad mortgage value is confirmed at $100. Buying at $99 and mortgaging yields exactly one dollar profit. I am now checking whether the game engine allows mortgaging a property immediately after purchase.
